title: Database and Persistence
readerIntent: Understand how Nodics persists schema-owned records without coupling business modules to a database vendor.
owner: Nodics provider-neutral database capability and configured provider modules
summary: Schema models call a provider-neutral persistence contract that resolves tenant and module context before delegating connection, schema, model, query, and transaction behavior to the selected adapter.

sections.heading: What is Database and Persistence?
paragraphs: Persistence stores business information so it survives a process restart. A database provider implements physical storage and querying, while Nodics schemas, item models, and services preserve the business contract independently of the selected provider.
Think of a governed records office: business teams use one approved records process, while the archive technology behind it may change without giving every team direct archive access.

sections.heading: Business outcomes
items: Keep business models stable while infrastructure choices evolve.
Isolate tenant and module data through governed database resolution.
Reuse generated CRUD, validation, access policy, middleware, diagnostics, and transaction contracts.
Extend a customer project with another provider without adding vendor branches to business services.

sections.heading: Authority
paragraphs: Business modules own schemas and business rules. The database capability owns provider-neutral persistence. Each adapter owns vendor connection and operation mapping. No adapter becomes a second schema authority.

sections.heading: Provider-neutral flow
items: The owning capability defines its effective schema and calls framework model or data services.
Persistence resolves module, schema, tenant, connection, and operation context.
The selected provider translates schema, query, index, middleware, and transaction behavior.
The provider returns normalized results and failures through Nodics contracts.
Business services remain unaware of connection-driver details.

sections.heading: Why direct database access is prohibited
paragraphs: A direct driver call from a business module bypasses tenant resolution, schema composition, middleware, validation, transactions, diagnostics, provider selection, and extension contracts. It also makes later provider changes expensive.
Even when a database is installed locally, AI, Profile, CMS, commerce, and customer modules define their own schemas but interact through framework models and services.

sections.heading: Connections and tenant placement
paragraphs: A deployment may place tenants on shared infrastructure or assign dedicated database resources. Connection resolution uses governed tenant and module context rather than browser-selected connection details.
The provider lifecycle opens only required unique connections, verifies readiness, creates effective models and indexes, monitors health, and closes owned resources during shutdown.

sections.heading: Transactions and consistency
paragraphs: Transaction behavior depends on the normalized persistence contract and the selected provider's proven capability. A module must not assume distributed transactions merely because one adapter supports local transactions.
Cross-capability workflows may require idempotency, events, compensation, reconciliation, or publishing boundaries instead of one database transaction.

sections.heading: Example: create an enterprise
paragraphs: Profile validates the enterprise and tenant relationship, then uses its framework model service. Persistence resolves the tenant-aware connection and the configured adapter stores the record.
Axis sees the API response only. Search indexing, audit, cache invalidation, and events occur through owned lifecycle contracts. No frontend or BackOffice registry receives direct database authority.

sections.heading: Production responsibilities
items: Credentials, encryption, network exposure, provider hardening, and least privilege.
Indexes, query plans, connection pools, capacity, latency, and resource limits.
Backup, verified restore, retention, archival, migration, and disaster recovery.
Replication, failover, retry, idempotency, and degraded-dependency behavior.
Tenant isolation, audit evidence, monitoring, alerting, and provider-qualified tests.
